MARTA KOWAL-BRANDT
DevOps / Platform Engineer
[EMAIL] | [PHONE] | [LINKEDIN]

PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY
QA Automation Engineer with experience building and maintaining CI pipelines, Kubernetes-based ephemeral test environments, and test infrastructure for multiple product teams. Delivered measurable improvements to pipeline speed and CI costs, and built observability dashboards that helped teams reduce flaky tests. Developing further in DevOps and platform engineering through hands-on Kubernetes, GitOps, and Terraform projects. Currently studying for the Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) exam.

TECHNICAL SKILLS
CI/CD: GitLab CI, Jenkins, pipeline optimization, dependency caching, parallel test execution
Containers and orchestration: Docker, Kubernetes, k3s, Helm
Infrastructure and automation: Terraform (personal project use), Ansible (basic), Bash
GitOps: Argo CD
Monitoring and observability: Prometheus, Grafana, Loki
Programming and testing: Python, Java, Selenium, pytest, pytest-xdist
Databases and integrations: PostgreSQL, GitLab API
Cloud learning: AWS free tier; EC2 and S3 basics

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE
QA Automation Engineer (Test Infrastructure) | Odrava Health Software | 2021–Present
- Own GitLab CI pipelines and ephemeral test environments for three teams.
- Built merge-request environments comprising an application, PostgreSQL, and seeded data, deployed via Helm to a shared Kubernetes cluster from GitLab CI.
- Configured environments to be automatically removed after merge or 48 hours of inactivity; QA and product teams use them to review features before merge, and end-to-end tests run against them.
- Work with namespace-level access on the shared cluster; the platform team operates the Kubernetes cluster.
- Profiled pipelines across three teams, parallelized test jobs, added dependency caching, and separated end-to-end tests into their own stage. Reduced average pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes and monthly CI runner costs by about 30%.
- Built a Python and PostgreSQL process to collect CI test results and created Grafana dashboards to highlight flaky tests by team. After teams addressed leading offenders, the flaky-test rate fell from 7% to below 1%.
- Wrote the internal guide to how CI works, which is used in onboarding.
- Mentored two QA interns in 2023.

QA Engineer | Brightmill Software House | 2019–2021
- Tested web and mobile applications for multiple clients.
- Introduced the first automated regression suite for the largest project, using Java and Selenium, and configured Jenkins to run it nightly.
- The automation replaced a full manual regression process that had taken two people three days.

SELECTED PROJECTS
Homelab k3s Cluster with GitOps | Personal | 2024–2025
- Built a three-node Raspberry Pi 5 k3s cluster, with applications deployed from a Git repository using Argo CD.
- Set up Prometheus, Grafana, and Loki for monitoring, Traefik ingress, and cert-manager for TLS.
- Provisioned infrastructure for a small Hetzner VPS using Terraform in a personal account.
- Technologies: k3s, Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Terraform, Ansible (basic).

Merge-Request Ephemeral Environments | Odrava Health | 2023–2024
- Created short-lived environments for merge requests, including an application, PostgreSQL, and seeded data, deployed through GitLab CI and Helm to a shared Kubernetes cluster.
- Automated environment cleanup after merge or 48 hours of inactivity, enabling feature reviews and end-to-end testing before merge.
- Technologies: GitLab CI, Helm, Kubernetes, Docker, Bash, PostgreSQL.

Flaky Test Dashboard | Odrava Health | 2023
- Collected CI test results in PostgreSQL and built Grafana dashboards showing flaky tests by team.
- Helped teams identify and address top offenders; the flaky-test rate fell from 7% to below 1%.
- Technologies: Python, PostgreSQL, Grafana, GitLab API.

CI Pipeline Speed-up | Odrava Health | 2022
- Profiled pipelines for three teams, parallelized test jobs, added dependency caching, and split end-to-end testing into a separate stage.
- Reduced average pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes and monthly CI runner costs by about 30%.
- Technologies: GitLab CI, Docker, pytest-xdist.

CERTIFICATIONS AND PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT
- ISTQB Foundation Level, 2019
- Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA): studying; exam booked for January 2027
- Terraform Associate: completed practice tests; certification exam not taken

critique.content_quality_feedback: This is a clear, well-structured, results-oriented CV with strong quantified achievements. The experience and project sections demonstrate credible progression from QA automation toward DevOps/platform engineering. The strongest content includes ephemeral Kubernetes environments, CI/CD ownership, pipeline optimization, observability, and measurable improvements in delivery speed, cost, and flaky-test rate. The main content limitation is that the CV is better evidenced for test infrastructure than for broader cloud infrastructure engineering. It also does not clearly distinguish production/team infrastructure experience from personal learning projects in every relevant area. The certifications section is truthful and appropriately labels incomplete qualifications.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The CV is ATS-friendly overall: standard section headings, plain text formatting, consistent dates, and strong keyword coverage for GitLab CI, Jenkins, Kubernetes, Helm, Docker, Terraform, AWS, Prometheus, Grafana, PostgreSQL, Python, and Argo CD. Parsing should be reliable because there are no complex tables, graphics, columns, or unusual section names. AI screening probability is moderate: the document will likely match DevOps/platform searches, but may rank lower for this specific role because Terragrunt, system design, networking, mTLS, SSL/TLS, security, cloud operations, and stakeholder leadership are either absent or only weakly evidenced. The phrase 'Cloud learning: AWS free tier; EC2 and S3 basics' is appropriately cautious, but it will not satisfy systems seeking substantial AWS experience.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The strongest alignment is with hands-on infrastructure automation around CI/CD, Kubernetes-based environments, observability, analytical problem-solving, documentation, and collaboration with QA and product teams. The candidate also shows AWS exposure through learning, Terraform use in a personal Hetzner project, and TLS-related work through cert-manager. However, the role is broader and more senior in infrastructure scope: the candidate's own notes indicate no professional AWS/GCP/Azure experience, only personal Terraform use, no Terragrunt, namespace-level rather than cluster-level Kubernetes access, no production on-call ownership, and only observer participation in two incident calls. The candidate material does not show mTLS, detailed network design, practical security work, IoT or remote-device integration, virtual machines, or backend/full-stack engineering. These are candidate-profile gaps rather than CV-writing defects. The CV should nevertheless foreground the closest truthful evidence: secure TLS configuration in the homelab, infrastructure provisioning, environment lifecycle automation, technical documentation, cross-team adoption, and measurable analytical improvements. The culture alignment is credible through ownership of CI infrastructure, mentoring, documentation, and enabling multiple teams, but the CV does not explicitly use terms such as 'stakeholder alignment' or 'technical leadership' where the evidence supports a modest version of those concepts.
critique.improvement_instructions:
CRITICAL ISSUES: None identified. The CV is consistent with the Original Candidate Information, and the incomplete CKA and Terraform Associate status is represented truthfully.

TARGETED IMPROVEMENTS:
1. In the Professional Summary, replace the final two sentences with a more role-aligned but accurate summary that distinguishes professional and personal infrastructure experience. For example: 'Developing further in cloud infrastructure and platform engineering through hands-on Kubernetes, GitOps, Terraform, and observability projects. Professional experience includes owning CI/CD and Kubernetes-based ephemeral test environments for three teams; cloud exposure includes AWS EC2/S3 learning and Terraform provisioning of a personal Hetzner VPS.' This makes the relevant evidence easier for recruiters and ATS systems to identify without overstating cloud experience.
2. In the Technical Skills section, change 'Infrastructure and automation: Terraform (personal project use), Ansible (basic), Bash' to 'Infrastructure as Code and automation: Terraform (personal project use), Ansible (basic), Bash' so the ATS can associate Terraform with infrastructure-as-code while preserving the limitation.
3. In the Technical Skills section, change 'Cloud learning: AWS free tier; EC2 and S3 basics' to 'Cloud: AWS free tier learning (EC2, S3 basics); Hetzner VPS provisioned with Terraform for a personal project.' This presents the full truthful cloud-related evidence in one searchable line and avoids implying professional AWS operation.
4. In the Professional Experience section under Odrava Health Software, revise 'Own GitLab CI pipelines and ephemeral test environments for three teams' to 'Own GitLab CI pipelines and the delivery and lifecycle automation of ephemeral test environments used by three teams.' This more directly reflects infrastructure engineering and operation without claiming ownership of the shared Kubernetes cluster.
5. In the same Odrava experience section, add a truthful collaboration sentence after the environment bullets: 'Partner with QA and product teams to make environments available for feature review and end-to-end testing before merge.' This surfaces stakeholder collaboration and interface coordination already evidenced by the document.
6. In the same Odrava experience section, revise 'Wrote the internal guide to how CI works, which is used in onboarding' to 'Led the documentation of the internal CI operating model; the guide is used to onboard engineers and explain pipeline responsibilities and workflows.' Use this only as a wording improvement: it does not claim formal technical leadership, but better matches the ad's emphasis on leading technical topics and clear communication.
7. In the Selected Projects section under 'Homelab k3s Cluster with GitOps,' expand the TLS bullet to: 'Configured cert-manager for TLS certificate management and Traefik ingress; set up Prometheus, Grafana, and Loki for monitoring.' This makes the existing TLS and certificate-management evidence more visible to ATS screening. Do not add mTLS, network design, or security claims because they are not supported by the candidate information.
8. In the same homelab project, revise 'Provisioned infrastructure for a small Hetzner VPS using Terraform in a personal account' to 'Provisioned a small Hetzner VPS with Terraform in a personal account and maintained applications through GitOps on a three-node k3s cluster.' This gives the project a clearer infrastructure design and operation focus while remaining accurate.
9. In the Certifications and Professional Development section, keep the current truthful status wording, but make the distinction more ATS-readable by formatting the entries as: 'Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) — exam booked for January 2027; not yet certified' and 'HashiCorp Terraform Associate — practice tests completed; exam not taken.' This prevents automated or human readers from misinterpreting either item as an earned certification.
10. Before final submission, ensure that no unsupported terms such as 'Terragrunt,' 'mTLS,' 'production AWS,' 'cluster administration,' 'on-call,' or 'security engineering' are added merely to mirror the job advertisement. The current CV should emphasize adjacent evidence rather than claim these capabilities.

Claims the sources (the candidate's own material; for the employer, the job ad and company research) do not support:
- The automation replaced a full manual regression process that had taken two people three days.

critique.content_quality_feedback: The CV is well structured, readable, professional, and strongly evidence-based. It uses measurable outcomes effectively, including reducing pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes, reducing CI runner costs by about 30%, and reducing flaky tests from 7% to below 1%. The distinction between professional Kubernetes access and personal infrastructure work is appropriately transparent. The main content weakness is that the document presents a strong QA/test-infrastructure profile but does not yet demonstrate enough depth for a cloud infrastructure contractor role involving production cloud architecture, networking, security, and Terraform/Terragrunt ownership. Some project content is duplicated between Professional Experience and Selected Projects, which makes the CV longer without adding much evidence.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The section headings, chronological structure, bullet formatting, and plain-text technology names are ATS-friendly. Important supported keywords such as Kubernetes, Helm, GitLab CI, Terraform, Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, PostgreSQL, and AWS EC2/S3 are present. AI screening probability is moderate: the document will likely be recognized as a CI/CD, Kubernetes, and test-infrastructure profile, but ranking for this specific role may be reduced by the absence of Terragrunt, mTLS, network design, cloud operations, security, and production infrastructure terminology. The CV should make its supported TLS, ingress, certificate-management, and stakeholder-coordination experience more explicit without claiming unsupported mTLS or production AWS experience.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The strongest alignment is with hands-on infrastructure automation around CI/CD and Kubernetes-based environments, analytical problem-solving, observability, documentation, and collaboration with QA and product teams. The candidate also shows relevant systems thinking through the design of ephemeral environments containing applications, PostgreSQL, seeded data, Helm deployments, automated cleanup, and end-to-end test integration. However, the candidate's material shows significant gaps against the core contractor requirements: strong Terraform and Terragrunt, major-cloud infrastructure design and operation, mTLS, network design, practical security, and production ownership. The AWS experience is limited to free-tier learning, while Terraform is limited to personal use. There is no evidence of IoT, automotive, train-to-cloud, remote-device integration, backend/full-stack development, Linux administration, or virtual-machine operations. The CV is a credible transition profile for a junior or developing platform role, but it is not yet a strong match for this mid-level cloud infrastructure engagement.
critique.improvement_instructions:
CRITICAL ISSUES: None identified. The document does not appear to contain unsupported skills, certifications, tools, or experiences when cross-referenced with the candidate information.

MINOR / HIGH-VALUE IMPROVEMENTS:
1. In the headline, replace "DevOps / Platform Engineer" with a more precise truthful positioning such as "QA Automation Engineer | CI/CD & Kubernetes Test Infrastructure" or "Platform Engineering-Focused QA Automation Engineer." This avoids implying established cloud infrastructure seniority while still targeting the role's platform focus.
2. In the Professional Summary, make the supported systems-design and stakeholder evidence more prominent. For example, revise the opening to state that the candidate "designs and operates Kubernetes-based ephemeral test environments integrating application services, PostgreSQL, seeded data, Helm, GitLab CI, automated lifecycle management, and end-to-end testing for three teams." Retain the existing qualification that the Kubernetes cluster is operated by the platform team.
3. In the Technical Skills section, add the supported networking and security-adjacent terms under an appropriate line: "Networking and TLS: Traefik ingress; cert-manager; TLS certificate management." Do not add mTLS, network design, firewalling, or security engineering because those are not supported by the candidate information.
4. Keep the strongest quantified bullets in Professional Experience and shorten the corresponding project entries to one or two lines, preserving the technologies and outcomes. This will improve scanability and reduce repetition.
6. critique.content_quality_feedback: This is a strong, well-structured, metrics-driven CV with clear evidence of Kubernetes test infrastructure, CI/CD ownership, automation, observability, stakeholder collaboration, and measurable results. The project section reinforces the most relevant work and makes the career transition toward DevOps/platform engineering credible. The main content concern is potentially misleading certification wording: the heading “Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA)” may be read as an awarded certification even though the exam is only scheduled. The CV is also somewhat defensive in places, particularly the explicit “no professional AWS production experience” statement, although the transparency is valuable.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The CV is ATS-friendly overall: it uses standard section headings, conventional reverse-chronological experience, searchable technology names, and quantified outcomes. Keywords such as Kubernetes, Terraform, Helm, GitLab CI, AWS, TLS, observability, PostgreSQL, Python, and infrastructure automation are represented clearly. Its likely AI/ATS screening probability is good for QA infrastructure, Kubernetes test infrastructure, and junior-to-mid platform/DevOps roles, but moderate for this specific contractor role because Terraform is personal-project experience, Terragrunt is absent, production AWS experience is limited, and mTLS is not demonstrated. The plain-text contact placeholders should be replaced with actual contact details in the final version, and the document should remain free of tables, text boxes, icons, graphics, headers/footers containing essential information, and multi-column formatting.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The strongest alignment is with hands-on infrastructure engineering around ephemeral environments, Kubernetes, Helm, CI/CD, lifecycle automation, observability, pipeline optimization, analytical problem-solving, and stakeholder coordination. The CV also supports the ad's emphasis on ownership and bringing teams along: the candidate owns delivery workflows, aligned QA and product teams, and documented the CI operating model for onboarding. Alignment is weaker for the role's core cloud-infrastructure scope: there is no Terragrunt, no demonstrated mTLS or train/device connectivity, no IoT or automotive experience, and no production AWS operation. The candidate's Terraform, AWS, and Kubernetes work should remain accurately framed as personal, learning, or namespace-level experience rather than production platform ownership. The document does not establish backend/full-stack experience, although Java is present through test automation. These are candidate-experience gaps rather than defects that can be fixed through wording.

MARTA KOWAL-BRANDT
QA Automation Engineer | CI/CD & Kubernetes Test Infrastructure
[EMAIL] | [PHONE] | [LINKEDIN]

PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY
Designs and operates Kubernetes-based ephemeral test environments integrating an application, PostgreSQL, seeded data, Helm, GitLab CI, automated lifecycle management, and end-to-end testing for three teams. Owns CI/CD and environment delivery, partnering with QA and product teams to support feature review before merge. Works with namespace-level access on a shared Kubernetes cluster operated by the platform team. Delivered measurable improvements to pipeline speed and CI costs, and built observability dashboards that helped teams reduce flaky tests. Developing further in cloud infrastructure and platform engineering through hands-on Kubernetes, GitOps, Terraform, and observability projects. Cloud exposure includes AWS EC2/S3 learning and Terraform provisioning of a personal Hetzner VPS.

TECHNICAL SKILLS
CI/CD: GitLab CI, Jenkins, pipeline optimization, dependency caching, parallel test execution
Containers and orchestration: Docker, Kubernetes, k3s, Helm
Infrastructure as Code and automation: Terraform (personal project use), Ansible (basic), Bash
GitOps: Argo CD
Monitoring and observability: Prometheus, Grafana, Loki
Networking and TLS: Traefik ingress; cert-manager; TLS certificate management
Programming and testing: Python, Java, Selenium, pytest, pytest-xdist
Databases and integrations: PostgreSQL, GitLab API
Cloud: AWS: EC2 and S3 basics through free-tier learning; no professional AWS production experience. Hetzner VPS provisioned with Terraform for a personal project.

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE
QA Automation Engineer (Test Infrastructure) | Odrava Health Software | 2021–Present
- Own GitLab CI pipelines and the delivery and lifecycle automation of ephemeral test environments used by three teams.
- Built merge-request environments comprising an application, PostgreSQL, and seeded data, deployed via Helm to a shared Kubernetes cluster from GitLab CI.
- Configured environments to be automatically removed after merge or 48 hours of inactivity; QA and product teams use them to review features before merge, and end-to-end tests run against them.
- documented the internal CI operating model in a guide used for onboarding.
- Work with namespace-level access on the shared cluster; the platform team operates the Kubernetes cluster.
- Profiled pipelines across three teams, parallelized test jobs, added dependency caching, and separated end-to-end tests into their own stage. Reduced average pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes and monthly CI runner costs by about 30%.
- Built a Python and PostgreSQL process to collect CI test results and created Grafana dashboards to highlight flaky tests by team. After teams addressed leading offenders, the flaky-test rate fell from 7% to below 1%.
- Mentored two QA interns in 2023.

QA Engineer | Brightmill Software House | 2019–2021
- Tested web and mobile applications for multiple clients.
- Introduced the first automated regression suite for the largest project, using Java and Selenium, and configured Jenkins to run it nightly.

SELECTED PROJECTS
Homelab k3s Cluster with GitOps | Personal | 2024–2025
- Provisioned a small Hetzner VPS with Terraform and operated applications through GitOps on a three-node Raspberry Pi 5 k3s cluster; configured Argo CD, Traefik ingress, cert-manager for TLS certificate management, and Prometheus, Grafana, and Loki monitoring.
- Technologies: k3s, Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Terraform, Ansible (basic).

Merge-Request Ephemeral Environments | Odrava Health | 2023–2024
- Created short-lived merge-request environments for feature reviews and end-to-end testing, with automated cleanup after merge or 48 hours of inactivity.
- Technologies: GitLab CI, Helm, Kubernetes, Docker, Bash, PostgreSQL.

Flaky Test Dashboard | Odrava Health | 2023
- Collected CI test results in PostgreSQL and built Grafana dashboards showing flaky tests by team; the flaky-test rate fell from 7% to below 1% after teams addressed leading offenders.
- Technologies: Python, PostgreSQL, Grafana, GitLab API.

CI Pipeline Speed-up | Odrava Health | 2022
- Reduced average pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes and monthly CI runner costs by about 30% across three teams.
- Technologies: GitLab CI, Docker, pytest-xdist.

CERTIFICATIONS AND PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT
- ISTQB Foundation Level, 2019
- Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) — exam scheduled for January 2027; not yet certified
- HashiCorp Terraform Associate — practice tests completed; exam not taken.

critique.content_quality_feedback: The CV is well structured, readable, and unusually transparent about the candidate's level of cloud and Kubernetes experience. It uses strong quantified achievements: pipeline time reduced from 38 to 14 minutes, CI costs reduced by about 30%, and flaky-test rate reduced from 7% to below 1%. The project section reinforces the most relevant infrastructure work. However, the document is primarily a QA/test-infrastructure CV rather than a cloud infrastructure engineering CV, and several claims relevant to the target role are either not demonstrated or are only partially demonstrated. The summary is somewhat dense and repeats information from the skills and project sections. There is also a minor professionalism issue in the lowercase bullet beginning "documented."
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The document uses ATS-friendly headings, conventional employment history, text-based content, clear technology lists, and measurable outcomes. Relevant keywords such as Kubernetes, Terraform, GitLab CI, Helm, Docker, PostgreSQL, observability, TLS, Prometheus, Grafana, and Argo CD are present. AI/ATS screening probability is moderate rather than high: the CV will likely be recognized as relevant to Kubernetes, CI/CD, test infrastructure, and junior-to-mid platform work, but screening may reject or rank it lower because Terragrunt, mTLS, AWS production experience, security, system design, and cloud environment operation are not demonstrated. The explicit statements about no professional AWS production experience and uncompleted certifications are truthful and should be retained, but the CKA and Terraform entries should be placed under professional development rather than presented in a way that could be parsed as completed certifications.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The strongest alignment is hands-on infrastructure automation around ephemeral Kubernetes environments, CI/CD ownership, environment lifecycle management, observability, analytical improvement, and collaboration with QA and product teams. The candidate also shows relevant Terraform learning, AWS fundamentals, TLS certificate management, and technical documentation. The main gaps are strong Terraform and Terragrunt experience, production AWS or other major-cloud operation, mTLS, broader security awareness, system architecture and system design, IoT or remote-device integration, and Linux/virtual-machine experience. The CV does not establish backend or full-stack experience, although it does show Java automation experience. The role expects someone who can help design and take train-to-cloud infrastructure to production, while the documented experience is focused on test environments and namespace-level Kubernetes access under a platform team's cluster ownership. These are candidate-experience gaps rather than problems that can be fixed by wording alone.
critique.improvement_instructions:
CRITICAL ISSUES:
1. In the Certifications and Professional Development section, separate completed credentials from uncompleted development items. Keep "ISTQB Foundation Level, 2019" under a heading such as "Certifications," and move the following into "Professional Development": "CKA exam scheduled for January 2027 — not yet certified" and "Terraform Associate practice tests completed; exam not taken." This prevents ATS or recruiter misinterpretation that CKA or Terraform Associate has already been earned.
2. In the Professional Experience section under Odrava Health Software, capitalize the first word of the bullet "documented the internal CI operating model in a guide used for onboarding" to "Documented the internal CI operating model in a guide used for onboarding." 
3. In the Professional Summary, make the scope distinction more immediately visible by changing the opening to wording such as: "Owns GitLab CI and the design, deployment, and lifecycle automation of Kubernetes-based ephemeral test environments for three teams, using Helm, PostgreSQL, seeded data, and end-to-end testing." Retain the following clarification that the platform team operates the shared cluster and that the candidate has namespace-level access. This presents the infrastructure contribution strongly without implying cluster administration.
4. In the Professional Summary and/or the Odrava experience entry, make the stakeholder and technical-leadership evidence more explicit using only existing evidence. For example, state that the environments are used by QA and product teams for feature review before merge, and that the internal CI operating-model guide is used for onboarding. Do not describe this as leading cross-functional architecture or production operations, since the original information does not support those claims.
5. In the Technical Skills section, keep Terraform under a clearly scoped label such as "Terraform — personal-project use" and keep AWS under "AWS — EC2 and S3 fundamentals through learning." Do not list Terragrunt, mTLS, production AWS, security engineering, Linux administration, virtual machines, or system architecture as skills because the candidate information does not establish them.

MINOR, HIGH-VALUE ENHANCEMENTS:
6. In the Professional Summary, reduce repetition by removing either the detailed cloud-exposure sentence or the corresponding AWS/Hetzner detail from Technical Skills. Keep the most precise version in Technical Skills and use the summary space to emphasize the strongest job-relevant evidence: environment design, lifecycle automation, observability, CI/CD ownership, and measurable reliability/cost improvements.
7. In the Odrava Health Software experience entry, order the bullets so the infrastructure scope appears first, followed by the measurable outcomes, observability work, documentation, and mentoring. This will make the CV read more like an infrastructure-engineering profile while remaining truthful.
8. In the Selected Projects section, label "Homelab k3s Cluster with GitOps" explicitly as a personal project in the title or first line, and retain the existing details about the three Raspberry Pi 5 nodes, Hetzner VPS, Terraform, Argo CD, Traefik, cert-manager, and monitoring. This is useful evidence of hands-on learning, but its personal-project status should remain unmistakable.
critique.critical_issues: No clear hallucinated skills or experiences were detected when the CV was cross-referenced with the candidate information. The CV accurately states the candidate's namespace-level Kubernetes access, lack of professional AWS production experience, and uncompleted CKA and Terraform exams. The main critical document issue is the placement of uncompleted credentials under "Certifications and Professional Development," which could cause an ATS or recruiter to misread them as completed certifications; this is addressed in improvement instruction 1.

critique.content_quality_feedback: The CV is clear, well structured, professional, and unusually strong in its use of measurable outcomes. The experience and project sections establish credible hands-on work with GitLab CI, Kubernetes test environments, Helm, PostgreSQL, observability, and pipeline optimization. The explicit distinction between professional, personal-project, learning, and uncertified experience supports credibility. The main content limitation is role positioning: the document is convincing for QA automation, CI/CD, and test infrastructure, but less convincing for a cloud infrastructure contractor expected to design and operate production cloud systems. It also gives limited direct evidence of technical leadership, systems architecture, security decision-making, or stakeholder alignment.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The document is ATS-friendly: standard section headings, simple text structure, strong keyword density, no problematic tables or graphics, and clearly separated skills and experience. It should parse well and has a high screening probability for QA automation, CI/CD, Kubernetes test infrastructure, and junior DevOps/platform roles. For this specific vacancy, AI/ATS screening probability is moderate rather than high because the CV does not contain Terragrunt, mTLS, production AWS, cloud architecture, or explicit system design terminology. Existing keywords such as Terraform, Kubernetes, Helm, GitOps, TLS, certificate management, Prometheus, Grafana, and infrastructure automation are relevant and truthful.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The strongest alignment is with hands-on infrastructure automation, Kubernetes-based environment operation, observability, analytical problem-solving, clear documentation, and ownership of technical CI topics. The measurable reduction from 38 to 14 minutes, 30% lower CI runner costs, and flaky-test reduction from 7% to below 1% are particularly persuasive. The candidate's material shows useful adjacent experience with AWS learning, Terraform on Hetzner, TLS certificate management, Java, and Linux-like Raspberry Pi infrastructure. However, the candidate has a substantive gap against the requirement for strong Terraform and Terragrunt: Terraform is limited to personal-project use and Terragrunt is not mentioned. There is also no evidence of production AWS/cloud operation, mTLS, IoT or remote-device integration, production on-call, or backend/full-stack development. The CV demonstrates components of systems design but not the broader production architecture and train-to-cloud integration expected by the role. The culture alignment is credible through ownership, documentation, mentoring, cross-team enablement, and collaborative use of shared environments, but direct evidence of leading proposals across backend and infrastructure is limited.
critique.improvement_instructions:
MINOR, HIGH-VALUE IMPROVEMENTS:
1. In the Professional Summary section, replace the opening sentence with a more ATS-readable and target-relevant version that remains precise about scope: "QA Automation Engineer with hands-on infrastructure automation experience, owning GitLab CI and designing, deploying, and automating the lifecycle of Kubernetes-based ephemeral test environments for three teams." Keep the existing sentence about namespace-level access and platform-team ownership immediately afterward so the scope is not overstated.

2. In the Professional Summary section, add one truthful sentence after the measurable-results sentence to surface systems-design and stakeholder-related evidence already present in the CV: "Designed the environment workflow around application deployment, PostgreSQL, seeded data, automated cleanup, and end-to-end testing; documented the CI operating model for onboarding and enabled QA and product teams to review features before merge." This improves matching for system design, clear communication, and bringing stakeholders along without claiming production cloud architecture.

3. In the Technical Skills section, change the heading "Infrastructure as Code and automation" to "Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and automation" and retain the existing qualification "Terraform (personal-project use)". This adds the standard ATS term without implying professional Terraform ownership.

4. In the Technical Skills section, change "Networking and TLS: Traefik ingress; cert-manager; TLS certificate management" to "Networking and TLS: Traefik ingress, cert-manager, TLS certificate management, HTTPS/TLS" only if HTTPS/TLS accurately describes the certificate work performed. Do not add mTLS, Terragrunt, or other unsupported technologies.

The current wording is already substantially correct; this is primarily a consistency and ATS-polish change.
